Lessons.Title: Building Quadratic Functions from Geometric Patterns
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: build a quadratic function from geometric area, explain two equivalent expressions from the same drawing, and interpret how multiplying dimensions yields an expression containing n². Original independently authored Edulytiks lesson aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U06:L03 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/6/3/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/6/3/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The official source previews the identity n(n+2)=n²+2n; here the independently chosen rectangle has a different width extension.

Original figure: an n-by-(n+4) rectangular garden grid with n whole-number rows and n+4 columns. Each unit square contributes one square metre. Total A(n)=n(n+4)=n²+4n. Either expression counts the same area: one uses full dimensions; another counts an n×n square plus four additional columns of n cells each.

Values for n1,2,3,4 are5,12,21,32 square metres. First differences7,9,11 and second differences2,2. The function is defined for positive integer grid row count n here, even though polynomial formula can be evaluated for arbitrary real n.

Student activity: draw two different decompositions of the same rectangle, explain why formulas agree for all permitted n rather than only sample values, graph first four values and critique a mistaken n²+4 area expression that omits the four columns' variable height. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for complete diagram, equivalence proof, accurate table and domain interpretation.

V13 publisher activity repair: U6L3 compares areas of three square arrangements, sketches expanding square patterns, and reasons about a growing step diagram. The prior rectangular n(n+4) model correctly illustrated a quadratic but was insufficient to represent the geometric contrasts and student-created growing figures. New figures here are independently selected rather than copied.

V13 original area-card task: for a large n-by-n grid (n integer at least2), Card A is the intact square n^2, Card B cuts out a nonoverlapping 2-by-2 corner for n^2-4, and Card C shows TWO separate n-by-n squares plus a disjoint 2-by-2 tile for 2n^2+4. At n=3 the areas are9,5,22. Draw and label all cards, justify why the plus/minus terms are areas, and reject n^2-2 for the 2-by-2 removal.

V13 independent growing patterns: expanding square pattern S(n)=n^2+3 has counts 4,7,12 at steps1,2,3 and327 at step18. Another growing rectangular-steps pattern T(n)=n(n+3)=n^2+3n uses an n-by-(n+3) grid, giving 4,10,18,28 at steps1..4; first differences6,8,10 are not constant, disproving the claim that a simultaneous one-unit increase in rows and columns automatically makes total area linear. Students produce cell diagrams and explain equivalence by distribution.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area of an n-by-(n+4) rectangle is product of side lengths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent expressions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distribution rewrites the same counted quantity without changing function.

KeyConcepts.Title: First-party decomposition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Geometry explains why a squared and linear term appear.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Split extended rectangle into square and strip.
KeyConcepts.Example: n² tiles plus four strips each n tiles.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating four extra columns as four cells
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Each extra column has n cells.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mistaking equal sample outputs for proof of full equivalence
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A structural distributive argument is stronger.

SummaryPoints: Quadratic functions arise naturally from geometric area patterns.
Factored and expanded forms describe the same rectangle.
In the original n×(n+4) grid A=n²+4n.
Teacher reviews diagrams, equivalent forms and domain.
